extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, journal editors, referees, and authors (especially in pure math)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and proposed procedures for improving peer review and guidance on what kinds of math papers to write, publish, and how to judge others' work (focused on pure mathematics and journal practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce a clearly defined quick opinion window (3–4 weeks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a very clearly defined quick opinion window of about 3-4 weeks. The referees asked for quick opinions can either decline or agree within 48 hours. It will only take them about 10-20 minutes to make an opinion based on the introduction, so give them a week to respond with 1-2 paragraphs. Collect 2-3 quick opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an initial triage stage. Keep it short (1–2 paragraphs), collect a small number (2–3) of opinions, and expect quick accept/decline of reviewing invitations (48h). Modeled after how high-profile journals handle submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quick-opinion requests anonymous
rubrics_metrics.description: Make quick opinion requests anonymous. Request the reviewers to assess how the paper fits the journal (better, worse, on point, best submitted to another area to journals X, Y or Z, etc.). Adopt the practice of returning these opinions to the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymize the quick-opinion stage and return the short opinions to authors so they can decide whether to proceed. Use this feedback to move to the second stage only by mutual agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: If rejected after quick-opinion, forward quick opinions to next journal (without reviewer names)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper is rejected or withdrawn after the quick opinion stage, adopt the practice to send quick opinions to another journal where the paper is resubmitted. Don’t communicate the names of the reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves reviewer anonymity across submissions and helps subsequent editors by sharing summary triage opinions while protecting reviewers and allowing new editors to collect fresh opinions if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict web availability during quick-opinion stage for top journals
rubrics_metrics.description: The most selective journals should require that the paper not be available on the web during the quick opinion stage, and violators be rejected without review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A limited temporary embargo (3 weeks) is unlikely to harm authors since submission confirmation can serve as priority; editors can decide how to handle attempts to publicly announce or present the work during this window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-stage review with authors' names revealed
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second (actual review) stage, the referees should get papers with authors’ names and proceed per usual practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the initial anonymized triage only for fit assessment; full peer review should return to standard (non-anonymized) practice in math according to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick opinion content: assess journal fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick opinions should address how the paper fits the journal (better, worse, on point, or suggested alternative venues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the scope narrow: an assessment of topical fit and relative suitability rather than a full referee report; return this guidance to authors to inform next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t over-collect quick opinions (editorial bias warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: If as an editor you feel you need more [than 2-3 quick opinions], you are probably biased against the paper or the area, and are fishing for a negative opinion to have 'quick reject'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the number of quick-opinion requests to avoid biased fishing for negative reviews; reflect on editorial motives when requesting extra opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write papers that support a good colloquium-style talk
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end, you need to be able to give a good colloquium style talk about your work. Papers that enable such a talk typically: (a) solve a major open problem, (b) are part of a coherent 'series' that tells a story, or (c) are small but paired with exceptional lecturing ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding what to write/publish, focus on work that either stands alone as a major result, contributes to a coherent narrative across multiple papers, or pairs with demonstrated excellence in exposition and lecturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer coherent series over many one-off papers
rubrics_metrics.description: If your little paper fits the narrative, do write it and publish it. If it’s a one-off disconnected piece, it may distract from the story you want to tell about your main line of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider long-term career storytelling (job talks, research narrative) when choosing whether to publish small results; avoid building a CV of unrelated one-off papers unless that breadth is what you want to signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge papers on validity and importance supplemented by author/community context
rubrics_metrics.description: First, read the paper and judge validity and relative importance. Then supplement that judgement with what you know about the author and how their previous work was received by the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because expertise is fragmented and community acceptance matters, editors/referees should use both the technical merits and signals from the author's publication record and community reception to judge contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for cliques, cartels, and publication-inflation strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to strategies that inflate paper counts: forming close coauthor cliques, inventing an area and creating journals/conferences/proceedings, publishing heavily in little-known or poorly managed journals, organizing special issues, or using editorial positions to publish many papers with collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices may not be formally unethical under AMS/NAS definitions but are quantitatively abusive and harmful; editors and evaluators should scrutinize citation patterns, venue quality, repeated collaborator lists, and editorial roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid referees with close connections to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: When you need a referee, look at previous papers by the authors and ensure referees are not from their clique and are completely unrelated to them in any way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select referees with no evident collaboration ties; check author coauthor networks to avoid conflicts of interest and confirmation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring/postdoc selection: match candidate profile to institutional needs
rubrics_metrics.description: For hiring/postdoc decisions, weigh breadth versus depth: a candidate with many diverse papers may be better for institutions needing collaborative adaptability, while a candidate with fewer, coherent papers may suit roles emphasizing close supervision and building a research program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide based on the role's expectations (independence and breadth vs focused mentorship and coherent research agenda). Use proposal quality and best papers as key inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and respond to 'zero-knowledge publishing' patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of 'zero-knowledge publishing' include publishing many interconnected but opaque papers that claim equivalences/reductions among many problems (some correct, some incorrect), using different coauthor mixes to create credibility, and producing barely readable papers so referees miss errors. If detected, treat the corpus with skepticism until a definitive, clear, and correct paper appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for patterns of many near-equivalent claims, opaque exposition, selective famous coauthors, and later-emerging retractions; recommend ignoring the author(s) until a clear, definitive result is published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement modest, gradual changes to peer review starting in low-stakes venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about large changes; small changes can be helpful if implemented gradually and slowly. Example: TCS introduced double-blind review and a rebuttal process by starting in lesser-known, low-stakes conferences and iterating until kinks (like COI) were worked out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot innovations in smaller venues, learn from experience, fix issues, then scale up rather than introducing sweeping reforms in top journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community signals (previous acceptances, citations) when assessing novelty/utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at how previous papers by the author have been accepted by the community (venues, citations, retractions) to judge whether a short paper is likely to be a useful contribution or merely noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community acceptance and discoverability matter for usefulness; if a line of small papers is heavily self-citing and obscure, it may not be valuable despite being formally publishable.
